content.text:
# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original picture at the easel, a simulator of watercolor
on paper. The subject, setting and composition are yours to invent.
Work from knowledge and the notes in your studio; don't use reference
images or image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift workable
  paint with a damp brush using `b:lift(path)`.
- You mix your own paint from the 36 library pigments with `b:load`, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(seconds)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md; notes/watercolor_techniques.md;
notes/research/watercolor_physics.md as needed.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch sheet beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended paper after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: paper and wetness, recipe ratios, water, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

# Watercolor easel

The studio has five MCP tools: `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`.
`paint` runs a chunk of Lua. A chunk that succeeds keeps the paper, your
named brush loads and the material clock for the next chunk. A chunk that
fails leaves the committed painting as it was. Each chunk starts in a fresh
Lua VM: get your saved brushes back by name, and define your Lua variables
and functions again.

In the examples below, `<pigment>` stands for an id from `palette()`. Other
numbers in the examples show how a call is written; the values are yours to
choose.

## Paper and coordinates

```lua
paper{width=<cells>, height=<cells>, kind="<kind>", seed=<seed>}
```

- `width` and `height`: the sheet's size in simulation cells. Width accepts
  integers from 2 to 2,400 and height from 2 to 1,600.
- `kind`: `"cold-press"`, `"hot-press"` or `"rough"`.
- `seed`: an integer from 0 to 4,294,967,295.

The defaults are width 1,056, height 704, `"cold-press"` and seed 71, so
`paper{}` makes that sheet. The paper is created once; a continuation chunk
paints on the existing sheet.

Coordinates and brush widths are in cells. The origin is the upper-left
corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Fractional coordinates are
allowed. The sheet's kind and seed set its tooth. The Watercolor Lab
simulation runs on a hardware GPU.

## Palette and brushes

`palette()` returns the ids of all 36 pigments in the library. Use those
exact strings in `b:load`. Each pigment carries its library values for
absorption, scattering, granulation, staining and density. A load mixes the
optical coefficients and material properties of its pigments in proportion
to the amounts still in the brush.

```lua
b = brush{name="<name>", width=<cells>}
```

This makes a named round brush. Width accepts 1 to 2,400 cells and defaults
to 24. Pressure changes the contact radius around that nominal width.
Calling `brush{name="<name>"}` again gets back its saved width and load; to
change the width, use a new name. A name has up to 80 letters, digits, `-`,
`_` and `.`. It can't start with `.`.

```lua
b:load{water=<microliters>, pigments={["<pigment>"]=<amount>}}
```

A load adds to what the brush already holds. Each call takes 0 to 100
microliters of water and 0 to 10 arbitrary mass units of each pigment, and
can load several pigments together. The brush holds a finite amount and
keeps what it hasn't laid between strokes and chunks. `b:status()` reports
its `width` and its remaining `water` and `pigments`. A new name gives a
clean, empty brush.

## Marks and water

```lua
b:stroke({{x, y}, {x, y}, ...}, {pressure=<0..1>, duration=<seconds>})
```

A stroke takes a path of 1 to 2,000 points; a one-point path makes a round
contact. Pressure takes 0 to 1 and defaults to 0.35. A point can also be
`{x, y, pressure, time_seconds}`; point times start at zero and increase
along a moving path. Duration takes up to 600 seconds and must be positive
for a moving stroke. By default a stroke lasts its path length divided by
800 cells per second, with a minimum of 0.0625 seconds.

Water moves and dries during a stroke as its contacts are laid. `dry=true`
makes a dry contact and keeps the brush's water. A brush holding less than
0.001 microliters of water also makes a dry contact. `grade=<ratio>`, from
0 to 1, reduces the pigment from the top of a stroke to the bottom; 1 is an
even load.

`b:wash{x=, y=, width=, height=, grade=}` lays a rectangle as rows of brush
strokes. Its coordinates and dimensions are in cells. It takes the same
pressure, dry-contact, grade and duration options. The brush can run out of
water or pigment before it covers the whole area.

`drop{x=, y=, water=<microliters>, radius=<cells>}` adds clean water: 0 to
100 microliters over a radius of 1 to 1,200 cells, 12 by default. Water can
move workable paint and make a backrun.

`b:lift(path)` lays the round lift contact along a path of the same form.
It supplies water from the brush, loosens workable pigment on the sheet and
removes some suspended pigment from the sheet. Removed pigment is not added
to the brush's inventory. Cured paint has become part of the paper and
can't be lifted. `blot` and salt are unavailable here.

## Time and drying

`wait(seconds)` advances the material clock by 0 to 600 seconds a call and
returns the clock reading. `clock()` includes any fraction still waiting for
the next 0.0625-second tick. Each tick runs 11 or 12 Lab substeps, 180 per
painter-clock second on average. Looking and wall-clock time between calls
leave the material alone: the sheet stays as it was at the end of the last
call.

On the default paper, a test stroke on the Mac GPU became damp after about
1 second of further `wait` and dry after about 2.5 seconds, sampled every
0.25 seconds. It was a 150-cell stroke with a round brush of width 42 at
the default pressure 0.35, loaded with 10 microliters of water and 10 mass
units of French Ultramarine. The brush still held pigment when the stroke
ended. For a stroke like that, the wet-into-wet window is roughly the
first second of further painter-clock time. Earlier contacts in a stroke
have begun drying while the later ones are being laid.

Drying depends on the amount of water, the paper and the surrounding wet
area. A wetter area can stay workable longer.

`balance()` reports `dry`, `max_surface_water` and `max_wetness`, along with
diagnostics for the water and brush-release inventory. Standing surface
water at or below 0.002, with wetness remaining, counts as damp. `dry`
becomes true when wetness is below 0.02 everywhere and suspended pigment is at or
below 0.0001 per cell. The Lab reference uses half-float fields and
advection; `conserved` is false. The diagnostic totals don't promise
exact per-pigment conservation.

`glaze()` checks that the sheet is dry and refuses while it is wet. The
Lab engine already cures dry pigment into the paper's reflectance, so the
call adds no layer.

## Looking and the journal

The `look` tool returns a PNG of the paper as it is now. You see Color by
default. `mode: "gallery"` shows it in Gallery light (azimuth 115°,
elevation 55°, intensity 1) and `mode: "relief"` in raking light (135°,
25°, 1). A Color look also writes display-only Gallery and Relief
companions for the studio viewer, which shows Gallery light by default.
Looking changes neither the material nor the clock.

`size` sets the long side of a whole-sheet look, from 16 to 2,400 pixels.
Without it, the view has one pixel per cell. `crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1"` gives two
opposite corners in integer cells and returns that region at 1:1. The `look`
tool takes `mode`, `size`, `crop` and `scratch`.

Within Lua, `look{path="<name>.png", mode="color", width=<pixels>}` writes a
PNG into the studio, from 1 to 2,400 pixels wide. A Lua crop is
`crop={x, y, width, height}` in output pixels. `save("<name>.json")`
captures the sheet, the clock and the brush loads under that name. Every
successful chunk also saves an automatic checkpoint, which the next chunk
loads. A chunk whose exact source has already run is refused, so each
continuation needs new code.

`note` appends an entry to `notes/journal.md`, stamped with the painting's
time. To revise an entry, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage
to change, which must appear there once, and `text`, what takes its
place. `status` reports the setup and the clock. `log` returns the
successful Lua chunks in order; they are also kept in
`paintings/lua/painting.lua`.

## The scratch paper

Beside the painting stands scratch paper for trying out a mix, a stroke,
a glaze or a drying time before it goes on the painting. `paint`, `look`,
`status` and `log` work on it with `scratch: true`; without it they work on
the painting.

- The first use sets it up as the painting's paper was set up: the same
  size, kind and seed. The painting needs its own `paper{}` first.
- It is a separate sheet with its own brushes, loads, clock and log,
  `paintings/lua/scratch.lua`. Load a brush again here. Nothing done on
  it reaches the painting.
- It keeps its own clock. Time spent or waited there doesn't pass for
  the painting, and the painting's time doesn't pass for it.
- To use what worked, paint it on the painting with the same handling.
- `new_scratch: true`, with `scratch: true`, puts the current sheet aside
  and starts a fresh one before the chunk runs. The old log stays as
  `paintings/lua/scratch-1.lua`, then `scratch-2.lua` and so on. Each has
  its final checkpoint beside it as `scratch-1.json`, `scratch-2.json` and
  so on, so an operator can render that sheet later.
- A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's
  conditions: lay the underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry
  as long as it has on the painting.

## Lua

Lua has the math, table, string and utf8 libraries, a 128 MB memory limit
and a budget of about two million instructions per chunk. Native painting
and waiting run outside that instruction budget. Keep the same runner build
when continuing a painting.

# Watercolor techniques at this easel

How the watercolor painter's techniques are done with this easel's tools, and
where the engine differs from real paper. `notes/watercolor_easel_guide.md`
says what each call does; `notes/research/watercolor_physics.md` says how real
watercolor behaves. What you paint is yours to choose. In the examples,
`<pigment>` stands for any id that `palette()` returns.

## Plan before you paint

- **Try it on the scratch paper** (`scratch: true`): a load, a stroke, a wash
  into wet paper, a lift. The scratch sheet has the painting's size, kind and
  seed, and its own brushes and clock. Lay the underlayer the trial will go
  over and give it the same waiting time as on the painting, then compare
  the two in a 1:1 crop. Paint what worked on the painting with the same
  load, path, pressure and timing.
- **Start a clean sheet** with `new_scratch: true` when the scratch paper is
  full or when a trial needs dry, untouched paper.
- **Look at 1:1.** `look` with `crop="x0,y0,x1,y1"` returns cells at 1:1,
  which shows edges, granulation and dry-brush breaks. `mode="relief"` rakes
  light across the tooth. Looking does not advance the clock.

## Paper

- `paper{kind="hot-press"}`, `"cold-press"` (the default) or `"rough"` is
  chosen once, before the first mark. In this engine the kind sets the
  height of the tooth (relative amplitude 0.3 hot-press, 0.72 cold-press,
  1.0 rough) and its fiber texture. Absorption, evaporation and capillary
  spread use the same settings on all three kinds; there is no sizing
  setting.
- `seed=` changes the pattern of the tooth. The scratch paper copies it.

## Time and the stages of wetness

- **The clock is fast.** Real paper takes minutes to pass from shiny to dry
  (the physics note's table). Here a measured stroke went from wet to damp in
  about **1 second** of painter-clock `wait` and to dry in about **2.5
  seconds**, sampled every 0.25 seconds. That stroke was a 150-cell round
  stroke on the default paper, width 42, pressure 0.35, loaded with
  10 microliters of water and 10 mass units of `french-ultramarine`. A wetter or
  larger area stays workable longer.
- **The stroke dries as it is laid.** Point times and `duration` are painter
  clock too. In a slow stroke the first contacts have begun drying before
  the last ones land. Give a stroke that should stay wet along its length a
  short duration.
- **Reading the stage.** `balance()` returns `max_surface_water`,
  `max_wetness` and `dry`. Standing water above 0.002 means some of the
  sheet is still wet; 0.002 or less with wetness left is damp; `dry` is true when wetness
  is below 0.02 everywhere and suspended pigment is at or below 0.0001 per
  cell everywhere. These are maxima over the whole sheet, so any
  wet passage elsewhere sets them. To time one passage, lay it alone on the
  scratch paper and step the clock. What a chunk prints comes back in the
  `paint` reply:

  ```lua
  for i = 1, 16 do
    local t = wait(0.25)
    local s = balance()
    print(t, s.max_surface_water, s.max_wetness, s.dry)
  end
  ```

- Wall-clock time between calls and looking leave the sheet as it was.

## Loading and laying paint

- `b = brush{name="<name>", width=<cells>}` makes a round brush; the same name
  later returns it with its remaining load. A new name is a clean brush.
- `b:load{water=<µL>, pigments={["<pigment>"]=<mass>}}` adds to the load.
  The brush releases water and pigment from what it holds, and `b:status()`
  shows what is left. The brush runs dry, and a
  stroke or wash can end before its path does.
- `b:stroke(path, {pressure=..., duration=...})`. Each point can carry its own
  pressure and time, `{x, y, pressure, t}`. Pressure widens or narrows the
  contact around the nominal width.
- `b:wash{x=, y=, width=, height=}` lays a rectangle as rows of strokes;
  `grade=` thins the pigment from top to bottom (`1` is even).

## Wet-in-wet

- **Wet the area first.** Make a fresh named brush and load it with water
  only (`w = brush{name="<new name>"}; w:load{water=<µL>}`); a used brush
  keeps the pigment it still holds. Lay a wash or stroke with it, or put down clean water with
  `drop{x=, y=, water=<µL>, radius=<cells>}`. Then lay the pigment while the
  area is still wet: for a stroke-sized area that is within about a second
  of painter clock, longer for a flooded one.
- **Charge a wet stroke.** A second loaded brush laid into a stroke that is
  still wet joins its water, and the two loads flow together where they
  meet.
- **Mixtures.** A brush carrying several pigments lays one blended color with
  the averaged granulation, staining and density of its load. Where two
  colors meet wet, each cell carries one blended set as well. Pigments in a
  mixture do not separate by density here.

## Edges and backruns

- **Hard edges.** Water evaporates faster at the boundary of a wet area, and
  pigment there settles out as it dries, so a stroke laid on dry paper dries
  with a darker rim.
- **Soft edges.** Lay the stroke into wet paper, or into the still-wet edge of
  the passage beside it, before either reaches damp.
- **Backruns (blooms).** Clean water or a wetter load added to paint that has
  lost its standing water but is still damp spreads into it and pushes
  pigment to a darker, lobed rim. `drop{}` is the direct way. The wetness of
  damp paper fades over time, so the window for a backrun is short at this
  clock. Find it on the scratch paper with the same load and wait.
- Water dropped on dry paint finds nothing to move (see Glazing).

## Granulation

- Granulating pigments settle into the valleys of the tooth, most in slow,
  shallow water. The texture is fixed into the paper when the cell dries and
  stays visible under later glazes. A taller tooth (rough) gives stronger
  settling. The engine has no separate flocculation; clumping shows only as
  this settling.
- The engine's library values, with its own thresholds for these words:

| Property | Pigment ids |
|---|---|
| Granulating (0.5 or more) | `yellow-ochre`, `cobalt-violet`, `ultramarine-violet`, `french-ultramarine`, `cobalt-blue`, `cerulean-blue`, `viridian`, `terre-verte`, `raw-sienna`, `burnt-sienna`, `raw-umber`, `burnt-umber`, `indian-red`, `buff-titanium` |
| Staining (0.65 or more) | `indian-yellow`, `pyrrol-scarlet`, `quinacridone-rose`, `alizarin-crimson`, `quinacridone-burnt-orange`, `dioxazine-violet`, `phthalo-blue`, `prussian-blue`, `indanthrone-blue`, `phthalo-green` |
| Opaque (scattering 1.2 or more): can cover the color beneath and lighten darker passages, depending on the load | `cadmium-yellow`, `naples-yellow`, `cadmium-orange`, `cadmium-red`, `cerulean-blue`, `indian-red`, `buff-titanium` |
| Light (density 0.3 or less): stays in the water and travels far in blooms | `hansa-yellow`, `indian-yellow`, `green-gold`, `pyrrol-scarlet`, `quinacridone-rose`, `alizarin-crimson`, `quinacridone-burnt-orange`, `dioxazine-violet`, `phthalo-blue`, `prussian-blue`, `indanthrone-blue`, `phthalo-green`, `sap-green`, `hookers-green`, `neutral-tint` |

## Lifting

- `b:lift(path)` lays water from the brush along the path and loosens
  pigment that has settled but not dried. The lift loosens pigment only
  where there is water on the paper, so load the brush with water and it
  brings its own. Its scrub effect fades within a fraction of a second of
  painter clock.
- Staining pigment resists the lift and gives up only part of its deposit;
  non-staining pigment lifts nearly clean.
- **Lifting loosens workable pigment and removes some suspension from the
  sheet.** Removed pigment is not added to the brush's inventory. Loosened
  pigment that stays moves with the water and settles again. There is no
  blotting (`blot` is unavailable).
- **Dry paint cannot be lifted.** Once a cell is dry its paint is part of the
  paper. Lift before the area dries.

## Glazing

- Wait until `balance().dry` is true (or `glaze()` succeeds; it refuses while
  the sheet is wet). A stroke over dry paint then lays a new
  layer whose color combines with what is under it.
- Dried paint here does not redissolve: water and new paint over it leave it
  as it is, so a glaze never stirs the layer beneath. Real paint can
  redissolve and tint the new layer (the physics note's staining section).
- Opaque pigments can cover the color beneath and lighten darker passages;
  how much depends on the load. Transparent ones let what is under them show
  through. Try a glaze over the same
  underlayer on the scratch paper first.

## Dry brush

- `b:stroke(path, {dry=true})`, or a brush with almost no water left, makes
  dry contact: pigment lands on the high points of the tooth and skips the
  valleys. The brush keeps its water. The paper's kind and seed decide
  where the stroke breaks.
- Pressure changes the contact width. Check the mark in a 1:1 crop and in
  `relief`, on the scratch paper first.

## Limits of this engine

- **One dried layer.** Every dried pass folds into a single paper
  reflectance. The engine keeps no separate glaze layers and no record of
  which pigment lies where once it has dried.
- **No blotting** and no salt. Neither call is available.
- **Pigment is not conserved while it flows.** The amount of pigment can
  drift as paint moves with the water; `balance()` reports
  `conserved=false`.
- **No sizing or tilt.** Paper kinds differ in tooth and fiber texture, and
  no call tilts the sheet or changes its sizing.
- **Fast clock.** Stages that take minutes on real paper pass in seconds
  here, so time wet work by `balance()` and scratch trials.

## Finishing

- Let the sheet dry (`balance().dry`) before the last look. The studio viewer
  shows the painting in Gallery light by default; `look` with
  `mode="gallery"` shows the same.

I'm puzzled that the water volume released seems fixed at 8.36 µL regardless of stroke length, with pigment depositing quickly early in the stroke and little water visible afterward — something about how the stroke distributes its load doesn't match my expectations for a 10 µL load.

I'm now considering that pigment amount, not water, might be the real limiting factor for stroke length, and wondering whether multiple load calls could stack to let me build longer strokes with higher pigment mass.

Testing shows water doesn't dilute the result at all — 40µL and 80µL of water with the same pigment look identical, so darkness must come from pigment decaying as it releases along the stroke rather than from concentration. That suggests I should write a helper that periodically reloads the brush to a target pigment level between short stroke segments, keeping color even across long strokes.

arguments.lua:
local function top(b,W,mix)
  local s=b:status()
  local add={}
  for k,v in pairs(mix) do local have=s.pigments[k] or 0; if v>have then add[k]=math.min(10,v-have) end end
  local w=math.max(0,math.min(100,W-s.water))
  b:load{water=w,pigments=add}
end
local function longstroke(b,W,mix,x0,x1,y,seg)
  local x=x0
  while x<x1 do
    top(b,W,mix)
    local xe=math.min(x1,x+seg)
    b:stroke({{x,y},{xe,y}})
    x=xe
  end
end
local P={0.05,0.15,0.5,1.5}
for i,p in ipairs(P) do
  local b=brush{name="L"..i,width=30}
  longstroke(b,30,{["french-ultramarine"]=p},60,760,60+(i-1)*100,40)
  local s=b:status() print(i,s.water)
end
